The research systematically studies the interplay between perception and reasoning in VLM post-training by decomposing their capabilities into three separate training stages: visual perception, visual reasoning, and textual reasoning, incorporating specialized training data.

Recent advances in VLMs emphasize long chain-of-thought reasoning, but their performance on visual tasks is primarily limited by a lack of visual perception as opposed to reasoning itself.

This capability-based staging represents a new curriculum dimension orthogonal to traditional difficulty-based curricula, and combining both yields further additive gains.

## Overview

Visionary-R1 is an RL framework that improves visual reasoning in VLMs by using a caption–reason–answer output, curbing shortcut learning and boosting accuracy.

## The Problem It Addresses

Simply applying reinforcement learning to a VLM -- by prompting the model to produce a reasoning chain before providing an answer -- can lead the model to develop shortcuts from easy questions, thereby reducing its ability to generalize across unseen data distributions.

## The Solution: Caption-Reason-Answer Format

The model is trained to adhere to a caption-reason-answer output format: initially generating a detailed caption for an image, followed by constructing an extensive reasoning chain. Enforcing a caption stage before reasoning is the critical intervention to suppress shortcut learning in RL-trained VLMs.

## Performance Results

When trained on 273K CoT-free visual question-answer pairs and using only reinforcement learning, Visionary-R1 outperforms strong multimodal models, such as GPT-4o, Claude3.5-Sonnet, and Gemini-1.5-Pro, on multiple visual reasoning benchmarks.

## Key Innovation

The framework's core innovation is requiring detailed visual captions before reasoning, which forces the model to engage with the actual image content rather than relying on textual shortcuts, resulting in more robust and generalizable visual reasoning capabilities.

## MathVerse Overview

MathVerse is an all-around visual math benchmark designed for an equitable and in-depth evaluation of MLLMs, with 2,612 high-quality, multi-subject math problems with diagrams collected from publicly available sources.

## Six Versions Structure

Each problem is transformed by human annotators into six distinct versions, each offering varying degrees of information content in multi-modality, contributing to 15K test samples in total. Specifically, researchers carefully adapted these problems into six distinct formats, ranging from text-dominant to vision-only.

The three main text versions include:
- Text-dominant: All descriptive, property, and essential condition information is in text, with the diagram present but potentially redundant.
- Text-lite: Text omits redundant descriptive details available in the diagram, shifting more "extractive" work to the model's visual perception.
- Text-only: The diagram is removed; all information is purely textual, serving as a test of models' non-visual (symbolic) reasoning.

## Research Findings

This approach allows MathVerse to comprehensively assess whether and how much MLLMs can truly understand the visual diagrams for mathematical reasoning. MathVerse was published at ECCV 2024 and has become an important benchmark for evaluating multimodal mathematical reasoning capabilities.

## NeSyGeo Overview

NeSyGeo is a novel neuro-symbolic framework for generating geometric reasoning data. To the best of the researchers' knowledge, they are the first to propose a neuro-symbolic approach in generating multimodal reasoning data.

## Core Components

The pipeline is built upon Geo-DSL, a symbolic DSL designed to represent most elements in plane geometry space concisely and wholly. The framework designs a symbolic–visual–text pipeline that synthesizes symbolic sequences, maps them to corresponding visual and textual representations, and generates diverse question–answer (Q&A) pairs using large language models (LLMs).

## Datasets and Benchmarks

Based on this framework, the researchers construct NeSyGeo-CoT and NeSyGeo-Caption datasets, containing 100k samples, and release a new benchmark NeSyGeo-Test for evaluating geometric reasoning abilities in MLLMs.

## Performance Results

With only 4k samples and two epochs of reinforcement fine-tuning, base models achieve improvements of up to +15.8% on MathVision, +8.4% on MathVerse, and +7.3% on GeoQA.

Based on the search results, I found information about the Chimera research on shortcut learning in visual-language understanding:

## Overview

Chimera is a comprehensive test suite comprising 7,500 high-quality diagrams sourced from Wikipedia; each diagram is annotated with its symbolic content represented by semantic triples along with multi-level questions designed to assess four fundamental aspects of diagram comprehension: entity recognition, relation understanding, knowledge grounding, and visual reasoning.

## Purpose and Findings

While recent evaluations suggest that vision-language models (VLMs) perform well on diagram-related benchmarks, their reliance on knowledge, reasoning, or modality shortcuts raises concerns about whether they genuinely understand and reason over diagrams.

The research uses Chimera to measure the presence of three types of shortcuts in visual question answering: (1) the visual-memorization shortcut, where VLMs rely on memorized visual patterns; (2) the knowledge-recall shortcut, where models leverage memorized factual knowledge instead of interpreting the diagram; and (3) the Clever-Hans shortcut, where models exploit superficial language patterns or priors without true comprehension.

When evaluating 15 open-source VLMs from 7 model families on Chimera, the findings show that their seemingly strong performance largely stems from shortcut behaviors -- visual-memorization shortcuts have slight impact, knowledge-recall shortcuts play a moderate role, and Clever-Hans shortcuts contribute significantly.

## Publication Venues

The research has been submitted to multiple venues: it was submitted to NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track and also submitted as an ICLR 2026 Conference submission (withdrawn).

## Overview

MAVIS is the first MAthematical VISual instruction tuning paradigm for MLLMs, involving a series of mathematical visual datasets and specialized MLLMs.

## The Problem It Addresses

MLLMs' mathematical capabilities remain under-explored with three areas to be improved: visual encoding of math diagrams, diagram-language alignment, and chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning.

## Key Components

The approach creates two datasets: MAVIS-Caption (558K diagram-caption pairs) and MAVIS-Instruct (834K visual math problems with CoT rationales), with four progressive stages for training MLLMs from scratch.

The training process includes:
- MAVIS-Caption is used to fine-tune a math-specific vision encoder (CLIP-Math) through contrastive learning
- CLIP-Math is aligned with a large language model (LLM) by a projection layer to enhance vision-language alignment in mathematical domains
- Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is employed with annotated CoT rationales to enhance the reasoning capabilities of the model

## Publication

MAVIS is part of the International Conference on Representation Learning 2025 (ICLR 2025) Conference, and the code is available on GitHub at the official repository.

## Overview

TPCL (Task Progressive Curriculum Learning) breaks the main VQA problem into smaller, easier tasks based on the question type and progressively trains the model on a carefully crafted sequence of tasks.

## Method Details

TPCL is a simple, model-agnostic framework that progressively trains VQA models using a curriculum built by jointly considering question type and difficulty, first grouping questions based on their semantic type and then ordering them using a novel Optimal Transport-based difficulty measure.

## Performance Results

Without either data augmentation or explicit debiasing mechanism, it achieves state-of-the-art on VQA-CP v2, VQA-CP v1 and VQA v2 datasets, outperforming the most competitive robust VQA approaches by more than 5% and 7% on VQA-CP v2 and VQA-CP v1 respectively.

TPCL (Task Progressive Curriculum Learning) breaks the main VQA problem into smaller, easier tasks based on the question type and progressively trains the model on a carefully crafted sequence of tasks.

## Method Details

TPCL is a simple, model-agnostic framework that progressively trains VQA models using a curriculum built by jointly considering question type and difficulty, first grouping questions based on their semantic type and then ordering them using a novel Optimal Transport-based difficulty measure.

## Key Findings

Aggressive modality dropout can reverse negative co-learning (NCL) to positive co-learning (PCL). This technique can "prep" a multimodal model for unimodal deployment and dramatically increases model performance during negative co-learning, with some experiments showing a 20% gain in accuracy.

### How It Works

Simultaneous modality dropout involves explicitly supervising all non-empty modality combinations every iteration, which is feasible for few modalities and enhances stability and missingness-awareness. Prevention of modality dominance through dropout precludes over-reliance on the "easiest" or highest-correlation modality, ensuring cross-modal cues are utilized.

### Benefits

Empirical studies in tasks as varied as medical segmentation, product recommendation, multimodal dialogue, speech detection, and action recognition confirm that modality dropout is an effective mechanism for improving robustness to missing, corrupted, or noisy modality data. Dropout regularizes the fusion space, acting as an implicit ensembling mechanism that widens the modal support of learned representations.

The recent research from 2025-2026 shows growing interest in this approach for creating more robust multimodal models that maintain performance even when modalities are missing during inference.

The GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) training aims to make vision language models solve math problems via RL (reinforcement learning) given image input. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) RL uses rule-based rewards tailored for constraint satisfaction and self-reflection.
